speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Several Members have filed Parliamentary Questions (PQs) on the Certificates of Entitlement (COEs).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: My Ministerial Statement will address Question Nos 1 to 7 for Oral Answer as well as Question No 25 for a Written Answer in today's Order Paper, as well as related questions that have been filed for subsequent Sittings.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To be complete, any discussion on COEs must be situated within the broader context of our land transport system of which private cars are but one aspect.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We must make it much more sustainable as part of the national effort to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Pre-COVID-19, about 14 million journeys were made every day, across four modes – public transport, point-to-point transport, private vehicles and active mobility.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Government's aim is to build an accessible, inclusive and sustainable land transport system that meets the needs of all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The best way to achieve this is through mass public transport.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It allows the greatest number of people to get to their destinations with the least land take and carbon emissions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In contrast, roads take up 12% of our land, for seven million journeys.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This includes those made by cars, motorcycles, buses as well as private hire cars (PHCs).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Compared to driving an internal combustion engine car, taking the train reduces our carbon footprint by 90%.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: That is why mass public transport is the core of our transport strategy and our rail network is the backbone of our transport system.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Today, seven in 10 households are within a 10-minute walk of one of our 202 Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) and Light Rail Transit (LRT) stations.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: By the next decade, it will be eight in 10 households.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: By 2035, we will have eight MRT lines and two LRT lines, interconnected and reaching all parts of the island.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As we expand our public transport network, we are also ensuring that it is inclusive, affordable and sustainable.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Today, all our MRT stations and bus interchanges, as well as 98% of our bus stops, are barrier-free and the work is ongoing.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Public transport, as we have discussed many times in this House, is heavily subsidised.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And our public transport fleet will fully comprise cleaner energy models by 2040.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We are also improving first-mile-last-mile connectivity with extensive infrastructure for cyclists and pedestrians.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Through the Land Transport Authority (LTA)'s "Friendly Streets" initiative, we will work with the local communities to create more pedestrian-friendly facilities within residential neighbourhoods.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: More broadly, LTA and fellow Government agencies are integrating land transport and urban planning strategies to enhance the liveability of our city by bringing jobs closer to homes, developing lifestyle and amenity hubs near transport nodes and making public transport and active mobility convenient for the daily commute.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: With excellent public transport connectivity and active mobility infrastructure, less road and parking spaces are needed for general vehicular traffic.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This is the "car-lite" future that we envisage as we plan and redevelop our precincts to prioritise pedestrians, cyclists and public transport users and lessen the need for and use of private cars.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Even amongst cars, there is a spectrum of choices.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Shared transport, which includes both taxis and PHCs, providing point-to-point (P2P) passenger transport services, complements mass public transport.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: They provide a useful alternative to car ownership for those who may need access to car-like services, whether chauffeured or self-driving.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Today, the P2P sector accounts for around one million daily journeys, up from 800,000 in 2012.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: With zero growth in our car population, such shared transport, including car sharing services, allows for a more efficient and inclusive use of our roads, serving the needs of many more Singaporeans, compared to individually-owned private cars.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The total PHC population has averaged around 70,000 since 2019, with some fluctuations due to COVID-19 and the subsequent reopening of Singapore's economy.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As a proportion of the total car population, PHCs have remained at around 10% for the past four years.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In fact, the period where we saw the fastest growth in PHC numbers was between 2015 and 2017, where they increased from 30,000 to almost 70,000.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: There was no commensurate upward pressure on COE prices in that period.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Conversely, while COE prices have been rising over the past several quarters, demand from PHC companies has, in fact, been moderating.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: PHCs are a flexible way to augment the supply of P2P passenger transport, giving commuters more choices while serving a much wider segment of society than private cars.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, we should be careful when making calls about imposing caps, sometimes arbitrarily, on the PHC population.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: That said, the PHCs are a relatively new development.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The P2P regulatory framework, for example, only commenced in 2017 and COVID-19 has caused some disruption in the market.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We are studying this further to ascertain the effect of PHCs and whether there is, in fact, any impact on the market.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: On private car ownership, there are encouraging trends, especially amongst our youths.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: More than 75% of the respondents cited ready access to public transport as the reason why they did not aspire to own a car.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Nevertheless, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, we do recognise that there is still a desire to own a car.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: For some, it is a necessity; for others, a useful option; yet others, an aspiration.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Hence, it is quite understandable that Members have raised questions on COEs and prices.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: COEs are a key feature of our Vehicle Quota System (VQS).

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The VQS is essential for us to achieve our zero growth rate policy objective for cars and motorcycles.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It is the principal tool to manage ownership, as recognised in the 1996 White Paper on creating "A World Class Land Transport System".

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The VQS fundamentally works through supply and demand forces to efficiently allocate a scarce resource – COEs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The system also incorporates progressivity considerations by having different COE categories.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In fact, when the COE system first started in 1990, there were four categories for cars.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The number of categories was reduced to the current two in 1999 to address concerns over the relatively small quota supply and resultant volatility as well as limited choices of cars in some categories.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Category E (Cat E), which is the Open category, was retained to allow for changing preferences and needs in vehicle types over time.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa has asked if there are plans to review the COE system.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: On the whole, the system continues to serve our policy objective of efficiently allocating the limited supply of COEs.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: However, over the years, the Ministry of Transport (MOT) and LTA have made various refinements to the VQS scheme to ensure its relevance and efficacy without forsaking the core policy intent.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The power rating criterion of 97 kilowatt (kW) was introduced in 2014 for the mass market Cat A, so that car COE categories are differentiated not just by engine capacity.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Last year, as more electric car models became available in Singapore, we increased the power output threshold for Cat A COEs to 110 kilowatt hour (kWh) in order to accommodate mass market electric cars.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In other words, if I can put it the other way, Cat B OMVs in the median is about 75% higher compared to the median in Cat A.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, there is a clear differentiation although it may not be a complete dichotomisation of the market.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We will continue to monitor and review the differentiating criteria between Categories A and B as the technology evolves.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Ms Mariam Jafaar and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about Cat D COEs for motorcycles.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: A key feature of the motorcycle market is that dealers bid and hold the temporary COEs (TCOEs) in their own name before transferring it to a motorcycle buyer.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This is a deliberate design feature because it provides convenience for buyers who can readily purchase a motorcycle.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This is unlike the car market where bids are primarily in the name of the buyer.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The prospective car buyers who need immediate access to a car and, in other words, a bid was not submitted in their name, can rely on Cat E COEs where there is some flexibility.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: To Ms Mariam Jaafar’s query, the expired TCOEs were held by more than 50 dealers; and of course, those with a bigger market share contributed more, but there is a spread.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The TCOE utilisation rates subsequently went back up, with the market correcting when it could not support the prevailing prices.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: This is what we mean by the market working as intended.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In other words, it responds to price signals, upwards or downwards, and then there is a re-allocation.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Dr Lim Wee Kiak and Ms Joan Pereira asked about the impact of foreigners.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The proportion of car COEs secured by foreigners remains low and has not changed significantly over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As I shared in January this year, from July 2020 to December 2022, on average, less than 3% of car COEs were allocated to foreigners.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Another common query – there is no specific PQ on this, but I know it is on many Members' minds and elsewhere – is about multiple-car owning households.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: In fact, over the past decade, the proportion of multiple-car owning households has been steadily declining from about 19% of households in 2012 to less than 15% today.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: I had also, in a response to a PQ earlier in the year, I think by Mr Gerald Giam, pointed out, and it is worth noting and underscoring that these multiple-car owning households reside not just in private residential estates, but also in public housing, including some households that own three or more cars.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked about the effect of car shows and promotions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As the Member would be well aware, consumers make their purchasing decisions based on a myriad of factors.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, it is actually quite difficult to establish a causal relationship between such car shows and promotions with COE prices.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, what then is the cause of rising COE prices?

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Demand in all categories has remained resilient, especially as the economy recovers from post-COVID-19.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Incomes have also been rising over the long term.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As was observed in Prof Raymond Ong’s article in The Straits Times on 7 May 2023, the ratio of COE prices to median monthly household income has fallen from 11 to one during the previous COE price peak in 2013 to nine is to one today.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: So, in comparison to median income, the COE price is actually lower – although in absolute terms, the price has risen.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: And the reason is because household incomes have risen.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As household incomes continue to rise in the coming years, coupled with our policy of zero-growth in the car population, we must expect the long-term trajectory for COE prices to be upwards.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: COE supply, in turn, is determined primarily by car de-registrations in preceding quarters, which have been relatively low of late.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Over the past few months, MOT has made several moves to reduce volatility in quota supply.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Instead of just the preceding quarter, we first adopted the average of the preceding two quarters in August last year and now use the moving average of de-registrations in the four preceding quarters to compute COE quotas for the next quarter.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: These moves have helped to mitigate quarter-on-quarter volatility.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: We also expect the COE supply to start increasing substantially in the coming months as more cars reach the 10-year mark.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Notwithstanding this, MOT and LTA have studied if there is more that we can do to smoothen the supply of COEs in Categories A and B, while adhering, importantly, to the cap on the overall car population over the 10-year cycle.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: As these five-year COEs cannot be extended and, therefore, have to be de-registered, LTA will be able to identify the exact number with certainty.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Even as we make this move, I would like to emphasise two points.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: First, this will help to lessen, but it will not eliminate, volatility in supply.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: There will still be a degree of supply fluctuation due to historical factors and also broader market conditions.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The COE system helps us to make our transport system more sustainable and our living environment better for all.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: The Government is committed to developing the necessary policies and infrastructure to build a car-lite, accessible, inclusive and sustainable transport system to meet the diverse needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: It is part of our social compact, anchored by the values we hold as a society.

speaker: The Minister for Transport (Mr S Iswaran)
text: Ultimately, our success in realising that vision rests on the commuting choices that every Singaporean makes every day.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: First, would MOT consider a pay-as-you-bid system instead of people bidding higher and then paying for the lowest rate?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Second, can we disallow financing of COE, which means that when you take a loan, it has to be only the car loan and not the COE?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I would say that that is not the source of the problem.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The issue is not the system or how it is being administered per se.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The issue is really around supply and some level of volatility that we are trying to mitigate, as well as where we can or where we discern some need to intervene because of either speculation or some inefficiencies in the market.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And that is what we have sought to do.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The second point on financing, I would say I think it is a question that should be put to the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), frankly, or the authorities.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But if I may just offer Members this perspective.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: A standalone COE is of little value until it is applied to register a car.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, one needs to look at it in totality first.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Second, if you look at it from the point of view of the cost of buying a car, which then you are seeking to finance, I think most financial institutions will look at it as a whole – the value of the car, the market price, including the COE price.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, that is why the system runs as it is.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Again, I want to go back to the point that I am not sure that decoupling the financing is going to be the solution to the current set of concerns that Members have.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: My first question to the Minister is, I think he mentioned that the reason why COE prices are higher is because of high demand and limited supply.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: But I would like to ask the Minister whether another reason why COE prices may be at this level, this recent wave, is because of the disparity in the purchasing power among the bidders.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In other words, there are, in each batch of the COE bidding, more bidders that have higher purchasing power and, therefore, the ability to pay up; and that is where the COE prices are.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I would like to ask whether that is desirable.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The second question is whether some amount of allocation by balloting, like how we do for housing, can be part of the solution as well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I am not sure what the Member means by disparity in purchasing power.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because, as I explained earlier, overall, if you look at it over a 10-year cycle, peak to peak, our incomes have risen.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And to the extent that cars remain an aspirational product or a necessity, then you must expect that there will be a propensity to want to allocate the budget to buy that and the prices will reflect, to some extent, the trends in incomes as well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is why I gave the numbers that I did.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is not to say that that is the only factor but, generally, if you compare it to incomes rising and so on, I think that does tell us an important story.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is about 36% to 37% – so, it is a very sizeable proportion of our population base.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, what we have been trying to do is, through a combination of ownership and usage measures, make cars available as widely as possible, but within our zero-growth constraint, which we have imposed for good reasons.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And that will continue to be the basis.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Member's second point was on balloting some amount.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I am very sure all the Members here will be able to offer perspectives on it, but let me just deal with this.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Do you price it at the same price as the COE in that period?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Or do you say no, it is a discounted price.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If it is a discounted price, then it is a windfall for the party that gets this, because they will then be able to resell the car with the COE at a higher price because the market clearing price is higher.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Then, the question is: what justifies such a ballot, who qualifies and how do we do it?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I am just sharing this with Members because I appreciate the intent behind the suggestion, but I am trying to point out that there are several, quite intractable, second- and third-order issues we will have to deal with.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And we will very quickly move from discussing COE prices to wondering why the balloting system is not working.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And, indeed, we do have discussions like that in this House as well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, a balloting system is not a panacea.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In fact, it may aggravate the problems, if the concern is around price and unevenness in the market.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One is in relation to the COE, whether the Ministry has conducted any public surveys to better understand and discover what are the factors that would persuade more private vehicle owners to switch to public transport.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Another one is in an effort to reduce carbon footprint, what is the ratio of the single- to double-decker buses currently in service and whether LTA has plans to move towards 100% double-decker buses to maximise ridership capacity and, thereby, an effort to reduce the carbon footprint?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Factors that will persuade the car owners to switch – there are several and I have talked about some of them.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But in the end, every individual is entitled to make their allocative decisions.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: What we are really trying to do is to make the alternatives as compelling as possible.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In fact, you hear this more from people who have lived overseas and come here.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I was recently at an American Chamber of Commerce dialogue.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And one of the ladies said she came from the US where she was wholly reliant on her car.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: She was waxing lyrical about our public transport system.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Her teenage daughter who studied here, used our public transport system, has since gone to the US for her further studies in Houston.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: According to her, the daughter laments that the public transport system in the US is not of the same quality and accessibility as here.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, we do have advocates and I am very keen to get more of such advocates, especially Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Many Singaporeans have told us that they really like the fact that we have a good public transport system.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Of course, there are always areas we can improve.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is also why I cited the survey – there is a perceptible shift in the preferences of the younger generation of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: They are more adept at using technology and some of the solutions already available.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: As a result, they are less seized with the need to buy a car.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In fact, they think there are other ways of using their money.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And I say, good for them, in that regard.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Single- to double-decker buses, I do not have the exact numbers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But I will put it this way – the move for sustainability is the thrust of the Member's question.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In terms of single- and double-decker buses, a lot of that is actually a function of capacity planning, based on the routes and the kind of demand.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This can vary, depending on how commuter behaviour changes over time.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, maybe a point-based system, where apart from the bidding price, we also consider other factors like nationality, and needs-based factors, like families with young children or persons with disability.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: A point-based system – it is really a variation of the idea that Mr Liang Eng Hwa talked about, a ballot.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because in the end, you have got to decide how you would allocate the points, on what basis?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And how will that then factor into the final COE allocation?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Does that mean that if someone has got more points, then they are entitled to a different price when it comes to the COE?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Or does it mean that they go into a different pool?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And if they go into a different pool, how do we segment the pools?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I think a point-based system has, in a sense, the kind of arbitrariness that we are trying to avoid.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is not unlike what we do, for example, for electricity in Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We do not say "first hundred units X, next hundred units Y".

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We price it all the same, because every one, from the beginning, is a unit of electricity.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But then what we do is that we provide U-Save rebates and so on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, if we want to help certain categories of people, it is best to do it that way.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Then, the Member makes a point about needs-based.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And I am quite sympathetic to her point, because many families say to me: "Look, I have got children and I need to take them around to enrichment classes on the weekends and so on, and public transport does not quite work for me".

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And then, we have others who say: "Look, I have got elderly parents whom I need to take to hospital or for medical appointments" and so on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think if you look at households in Singapore, they will either have children or elderly parents they have to look after and that will probably cover most households in Singapore.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, everyone has a need that I think we can understand.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The real question for us is: do we have the resources and the capacity to meet that need effectively?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I mean, I would be very happy if we had a cornucopia of COEs that we can just dispense at will.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But we do not, because of the constraints I have highlighted.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And that is why we have to make some tough choices in the allocative sense.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is one of the things we are doing and we will do more.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Also, some of the P2P operators, like Grab and so on, they offer chauffeured services where you can do block booking by time.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For example, if you want to take your parents to hospital you think it will take you four hours or whatever, you can make those sorts of bookings as well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, there are other solutions in place and I would say that that is something we should keep in mind.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The question is: what is the problem we are trying to fix here?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because you may come up with the tool, it may be a very popular move, but does it really address the problem at its root?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It has actually helped, in terms of price recovery and microstructure.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, in relation to our transition to move away from and finding alternatives to private car ownership, the Minister mentioned just now about enhancing the alternatives of P2Ps, PHCs and taxis going forward.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My question is that as we still have Singaporeans aspiring to own cars and we are trying to go car-lite, I think these are the sorts of issues that I am hearing from the Minister's Statement, we are not moving away from them anytime soon – car-lite, zero-growth, we are a very small country and the push is towards public transport.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is going to be a time transition for people to move away from their aspirations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: My question is: if you go towards the holistic approach or to the car-lite strategy and zero-growth, how can we improve our P2P, PHC and taxi services?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Because the exasperation of Singaporeans on the ground, if they want to move away from a private car, but they have to wait for taxis and PHCs and these are not there, every single minute when they want to have access to it, 24 hours of the day and at any time, is something that will need to be addressed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, I would like to get some clarification with regard to the five-year COE supply in terms of the numbers and what is the direction or thought trends going forward beyond the existing three to six months this year and probably into the many years ahead.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: In fact, the Finance Minister announced a whole set of moves to further increase the gradient and the progressivity.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I think those who are buying cars are actually going to be paying more and, especially if they are buying higher value cars or more expensive cars, they end up paying a higher amount in taxes as well.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On Mr Saktiandi's points, first, whether we can do more to increase the supply of the P2P, the private hire cars – and we use all these terms interchangeably – and taxis and so on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The bottom line is that we need to try all measures to enhance the availability of car-like – not car-lite – but car-like services.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because what people really value is the flexibility to be able to hop into a car and go to multiple locations in a certain period of time and come back.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But it is a waste to have the car sitting in the carpark when you are not using it for hours, when you only need it maybe a few hours in a week.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, we need to find more alternatives and that is what LTA and MOT are working on what we can do in terms of more in the P2P sector and the PHCs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I have a smile on my face because the Member is asking for whether we can do more and have more PHCs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think I have just heard from others advocating quite the opposite.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But the bottom line is, car for car – if I take a car away from private ownership and we put it in the P2P sector – it will benefit more people, at least, as a first principle.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Then, there are all the issues we need to deal with in terms of policy.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, we are working on a whole range of ideas on this, how we can do more.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And I accept the Member's point that there is a transition.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We already have pretty good connectivity, by the way; but this will take it at least a notch higher and we will be comparable to the best cities in the world.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, the key thing is to manage the transition.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And as I said, it is about populating the choice spectrum, giving people a whole range of options from public transport at one end to private car ownership on the other, and everything in between.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I think the more we can populate that choice spectrum and give people the information and the convenience to exercise that choice, then we are on the right path.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On the five-year COE supply, I think the Member's question is how it will be redistributed.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And it is not just for one or two quarters because LTA will be releasing more information.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If you go on the basis that everybody who is reaching their 10-year mark is going to de-register, then you are going to be at a peak.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because, essentially, it is, as one of my colleagues put it, a cut-and-fill exercise.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: You are really trying to smoothen the curve, try and avoid too sharp a gradient and, worse, the volatility, the ups and downs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is what we are trying to do.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But I want to emphasise again: this is not about therefore expecting prices to ease and that is the measure of success.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I have put out the information and I think car buyers as well as car dealers, based on that, I am sure their behaviour and the next and subsequent bidding rounds will be informed by this data.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And I think what sits with us is that we all feel that it is particularly egregious when the people who bear the brunt of these actions by dealers, are people who are the lowest income workers, students who are holding part-time jobs because they need to earn.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I guess my clarification is, can we do more to close down these loopholes a bit faster?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And three, is there a way to provide more transparency on individual dealer bidding practices?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: My second clarification is on car COEs this time.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Minister mentioned that they are currently still studying the impact of PHCs on COE prices.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, I want to just clarify, is there no evidence?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Does the Minister feel that there is no evidence today that the PHCs are driving up COE prices?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I mean the market works, but it is also not a level playing field as we know.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They have ways to pass on higher prices and also the ability to convert some of these PHCs into private cars, although, of course, there is a market for that.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, how can we close down some of these loopholes?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And can that be closed down as a low-hanging fruit?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: First, I want to just be very clear.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Member suggested that the moves we make affirm or confirm that there has been speculative behaviour and that that is what is causing the prices to go up.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The fact is the market has already been functioning and the way we know that is when the price goes up, as it did in some of the earlier cycles when the COE price for motorcycles went up to $13,000; and subsequently it came down, the market corrected.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Well, those who were left with very expensive COEs realised that they cannot sell the motorcycles with those COEs and they then had to give up the COEs or they forfeited them.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And we then have to recycle that into the market.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, there is a lag of at least 10 to 12 weeks before it goes back.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And what we wanted to do was to re-channel quicker.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, we shortened the validity period and then the motorcycle dealers can decide what they want.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Similarly, I do not think – whether it is $800 or $1,500, they are not arbitrary.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, there is a certain method in it.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Why do we exercise restraint and caution in raising the bid deposit?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If we inadvertently, through our policy moves, because deposits are very high, cause motorcycle prices to rise even further, then it will harm precisely the group that the Member wants to help.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And that is why we have been cautious about the way we have done this.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We may not be as fast as some would have liked but I think the yoke of being in Government and in LTA and MOT is that you have to exercise judgement and decide not just what to do but also how much and when.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And this is what has eventuated in what we are doing now.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But the market practice, in general, is that motorcycle buyers have a preference to just be able to go in and buy in the shops.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This is why we have had this arrangement for motorcycle dealers.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But there is nothing really that stops us from accommodating this and, in fact, we do already.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On PHCs, is there no evidence of PHCs driving up prices?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Well, I would like to draw the Member's attention to what I said in my Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I was not in MOT then, but there were not a lot of questions about it.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I do not think you can make an argument ex ante that there is a causality.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I understand that we are unhappy when prices go up.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But let us not be too quick to conclude what the causes are and, therefore, start fixing problems that may not really be at the root of the issue.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But having said that, I concede the point to the Member that the fact is, it is new and that is why I said what I said in my Statement.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: PHCs are a relatively new phenomenon and it is a very variegated terrain.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is not just your Grabs; you have got your car-sharing guys, you have got the rental guys who then lease to the drivers and so on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, it is important that we understand this correctly before we decide whether there is a need to act because they have an impact that perhaps distorts a market and then, if so, then what are those targeted measures.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And that is what MOT and LTA are studying.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I have some quick clarifications pertaining to public transport.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In the new fare adjustment formula, how is the productivity contribution quantum of 0.1% derived?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, leaving aside, for example, the recent periods when it is 12% or 13% and so on, if you look at in general, let us say you have a year when the fare increases 2%.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: When I extract 0.1% from you, if the fare increase is 1%, I am extracting 10% from you; 2% is 5%.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If it is a 3% increase, then 3.3% and so on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, it is actually quite a sizeable imposition on the PTOs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is not a free pass by any means.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The Member's point about whether we are doing more to work with them on productivity and other areas, absolutely.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is not something where we want LTA to just dictate and be left with it.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We see this as a joint endeavour and that is why many of the moves that are being made, in terms of technology, fuel efficiencies and so on, these are all areas that we are working together with the PTOs on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We are not recovering costs by any stretch.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, any savings are ploughed back into the system and it just gets distributed at large.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But the bottom line is that we are subsidising public transport significantly.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is not counting those who are on concession passes and those who are buying the concession fares; those who get concession fares and also the concession passes.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, by all accounts – and I think being very objective – we are making a strong effort to ensure that our public transport system remains affordable.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If you look at international comparisons, the answer is we are.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And if you look at our own pattern over time, expenditure on public transport, as a percentage of household expenses, actually, over the last 10 years, it has been declining for the quintile, decile, almost all the key metrics that we look at.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, my point is, we will continue to do our best to keep public transport affordable.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: When we get savings, it is basically ploughed back into the system.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We cannot do it at the particular service level; it has to be at the aggregated level.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But in the end, what really has an impact on the final expenditure incurred by the commuter is the subsidy that the Government gives, and that is not insubstantial.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I have a few clarifications on this five-year COE being brought forward.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The first is: is this just one-off to deal with the current trough or is this going to be a change in approach to how the five-year COEs are dealt with?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The second clarification is that I believe the Minister said they would be re-allocated to Cat A.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I just want to clarify, would they be re-allocated according to the expiring category or would they all be re-allocated only to Cat A?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The third clarification is I just wish to make the point that I think it is sensible to smoothen out the supply over the long term.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: LTA would not know how many five-year COEs will be expiring more than five years from now.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, what we know is the projection from now to five years from now and the latter part of that period coincides with the peak in the 10-year cycle.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is a very well-defined quantum because we have to bear in mind that the rest of the supply, which is dependent on deregistration, is really variable because it depends on whether people choose to deregister and, therefore, contribute back into the supply, or they may decide they want to renew their COEs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We do not know what will happen and that will then depress.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, the only component that we can deal with, with certainty, is the	five-year COE and that certainty is only available on a five-year outlook basis, and that is why we are doing this as a one-off, because it also serves a very important purpose of smoothening the supply from now, especially because now we are more or less in the trough of the 10-year cycle.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just two questions for the Minister for Transport and they are quite narrow, relating to the volatility or trying to manage the volatility in COE prices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, the first question is: with regard to car loan restrictions, which are now at seven years and at 70% of the selling price, is the Ministry intending to look at the loopholes vis-a-vis these car loan curbs, because it is not uncommon to hear of dealerships offering 100% loans and things of that nature.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second question pertains to the continuing relevance of the Cat E COE, the open category.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Unlike Cat A and Cat B, which we know are tied to car registration numbers, the Cat E COE can be traded for up to three months, if I recall correctly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, there is a potential speculative vector in Cat E COEs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Just to be very clear, we are not talking about volatility in prices.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is not the objective of the exercise.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: How prices eventuate in the market – as I have discussed and all of us know – is a function of various factors that are taking place.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Today, the prices may go down, tomorrow they may go up.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We think that the long-term trajectory is upwards for the reasons I have mentioned.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And the demand is a function, among other things, of incomes, and incomes are rising.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, if every time COE prices go up, we approach it as some kind of a new phenomenon, I think we should take pause and understand that these are the fundamentals that we are dealing with.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is a hard choice we have to make.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And the decision to have a zero vehicle growth rate is a very hard choice.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I just want to be very clear.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is not about price volatility, although that, I know, is a political concern.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is about supply volatility and how much we can smoothen that so that the market can function.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On the point on curbs on car loans, this should be a question answered by MAS.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Maybe I will allow my colleague, Alvin Tan, to reply.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Loans are under the purview of MAS and, if it is hire purchase, then I think it is under the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI).

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But the key point I want to make is that the moves we are making from the MOT and LTA perspectives are really in order to ensure the market functions as we intended and to smoothen the supply and that is why we are going for this.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: On the Member's second question on the relevance of Cat E, first, we need to size the thing correctly.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Essentially, we have had basically a Cat E component from the very beginning, and why is that important?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: When you have got these very fixed categories, you need a mechanism, a valve, if you will, that can help redistribute some because preferences may change over time.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: There may be a greater shift towards Cat A, there may be a greater shift to bigger cars, there may be other kinds of movements.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, it is at a level we, of course, as I have said, with COEs and the system, the Government has always been reviewing and constantly evaluating the relevance of measures.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But I am just trying to give the context for the Leader of the Opposition's benefit.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I do not think it is a purpose that is irrelevant in today's context by any means and for the foreseeable future.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But if there are some other efforts to think about the design of the system, then, at that point, maybe this can be revisited.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, the reason why you cannot say I create a valve but then I restrict its usage.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: If you cannot trade it and apply it to different categories and give them enough time to do that, then you may as well not have the category.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, the design and the features are tied specifically to the intent behind having the category.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Minister of State Alvin Tan, if you would like to contribute to the debate.

speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: There is a PQ by Ms Mariam Jafaar at No 64 on today's Order Paper.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I know this is an important topic for both sides of the House.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I propose to conclude this aspect of the business at the 60th minute mark.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, we have another 10 to 15 minutes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I have two supplementary questions on the Cat E COE.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: For the second supplementary question, I am very thankful that the Minister is using the COEs expiring in the next five years to reach earlier in the next few quarters.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The Minister has said that they will go back to the respective categories.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: So, I would like to urge the Minister to really distribute more to Cat A COEs because it is a mass market COE, whereas the Cat E COEs always mirror and always register for Cat B COEs.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: First, why does Cat C also contribute to Cat E?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because Cat E can also be used for Cat C.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That it is not the case today does not mean that it would not be the case tomorrow.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That is why I am saying that what we have to bear in mind is that the market has its own dynamic.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We do not know how things will go.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: People may decide that they do not like cars, they do not want cars and there may be a need more for commercial vehicles in which your Cat E will end up being used for Cat C.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Or people may shift their preferences to smaller cars because they want to be more environmentally conscious or spend less and so on.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And then, your Cat E could potentially go in there.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And, in fact, we do see some of those sorts of behaviours.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The point is, you must take from the categories to which the Cat E can apply and that is why we do this.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For motorcycles, for example, we do not do that.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: This was some years back and the reason is because you do not allow Cat E to be used for motorcycles.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, that sort of takes the motorcycles out of it.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is a necessary move and we think it will have a salutary impact overall on the system.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, that is why we are doing it.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And based on the numbers and what we can see, it should meet the objective of smoothening supply.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One is the whole discussion here actually is about prices going up too fast, too high and also about equity.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When prices go up high, many Singaporeans will not be able to afford.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second question is that, for the recent phenomenon we have seen in the motorcycle market, it has indicated that the Government does have some leverage on controlling the prices in the motorcycle COE market.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the recent collapse, I think it is a reflection that not enough has been done in the past.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Going forward, will the Minister say that the Government will be more careful because the price of a motorcycle is very important for many of our working Singaporeans; so, to be more careful in maybe controlling the prices of the motorcycle COE?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: When the Member said "be more careful", what does he mean?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We will prefer to have a lower price.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, if I may just ask one other question while the Member is at the lectern.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because I took considerable pains to explain this.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Does the Member agree that if the supply is limited, in fact, capped at zero growth, and incomes are rising, that the almost unavoidable conclusion is that the prices must rise?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Deputy Speaker, to answer the Minister, yes, we agree to many of the things that the Minister has said.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: For example, we have to control car population; as a result, we require the COE system to allocate the COEs, limited supply.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: However, I think the Government should also be careful when prices go up too fast, there will be problems, problem from the aspect of affordability and also from the aspect of equity.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, as a result, the discussion today is actually about that, that prices have gone up too much.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Like the motorcycle COE has gone up multiple times over the last two years.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We all want to help the people who buy cars and motorbikes.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I do not think you have a monopoly of virtue in that regard.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The real question here is, and if I hear you correctly, you accept that the long-term trend in prices must be up.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, now, your point is more about the rate of change and whether that can be something that can be done.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The only thing that the Government is able to do is settle on the supply and if there are any mechanics in the system, whether there are reasons to adjust them.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: How that flows into the market or works through the market is also dependent on demand, as the Member would know and, finally, the price outcome is how the market settles it.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: We know that the Cat D price has come down.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But does this mean that this is the new level?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, the sub-text here is that somehow it is foreigners who are buying it – because if Singaporeans cannot afford it, who is buying it?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I want the Member to be upfront about it because I have taken pains to point out again that the proportion of foreigners buying cars has remained low and stable.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, yes, what is happening is actually and the correct characterisation may well be that when the COE price goes up, some people will find it more difficult to afford; other people may find it easier to afford.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, there is a re-allocation and distribution going on within our society.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: It is a politically uncomfortable thing but it is a reality.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And I would urge the Member to be careful in the way he makes this point; otherwise, we give wrong conclusions and we end up distorting the discussion.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But having said that, if the Member wants to respond to this specifically, please do so.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The other point that the Member makes is on OMV and whether OMV should be used as a basis for categories.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: I had addressed the Member's point in my Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That means actually the market is already quite separated; I mean, you have the separation in terms of value.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: The next thing is we have achieved this or this is the outcome but the criteria, we are using our objective criteria – engine capacity, power output, what I have described earlier.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And our objective has always been to make sure that these criteria are able to accommodate the mass market models in the Cat A, as far as possible.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: That was one of the reasons for the recent adjustment so that the mass market electric vehicle models could also be captured.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But is there going to be some movement on the margin?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, you will see, as the Member has put it, some of the more expensive type cars migrating to the Cat A.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But by the same token, we also have what are considered generally as mass market cars that are actually in Cat B.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Examples will be some of the SUVs like Subaru Impreza and Mitsubishi something or other.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: Because of their engine capacity, two litres, they are in Cat B.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: What I am trying to say is that it is not a clean cut.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: And the problem with using an OMV, amongst other things, is that the OMV is not something that is objective criteria because there are a lot of other variables.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: For example, if exchange rates move, the OMV of the car changes.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: When we are making these recommendations, let us keep this in mind that there are many moving parts.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But the fundamental objective, which is the point that the Member is also driving at, we want to ensure that there is an element of progressivity in our COE system.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Leong, insofar as you are going to respond to the Minister's question to you, you are allowed to do so.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: And then, we will end with the last hand which I see, which is Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: So, Mr Leong, would you like to respond to the Minister?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: My question is about the equity amongst Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Minister mentioned that COE prices for the OMV value between Cat A and Cat B, there is a 75% difference.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But actually, that may not capture the whole picture.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, anyway, we are just urging the Government to further consider so that under Cat A, the slightly lower-income Singaporeans can still afford the cheaper cars.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just a quick point in response to the remark made by Minister of State Mr Alvin Tan vis-a-vis Mariam Jaafar's question for today's Order Paper.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It is directed at the Prime Minister and specifically to MAS on curbs on car loans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: As we know and as the Minister has alluded to, we also have car loans which take the form of almost like money lending or quasi-money lending arrangements.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: You have hire purchase, which comes under MTI.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Minister Iswaran, if you can close the business on this subject?

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: So, I wanted to be very sure about it.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: You do not need to pursue the matter.

speaker: Mr S Iswaran
text: But having said that, I just want to thank all Members for a very vigorous clarification session.
